To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the apparent concentrations of lithium in brain regions and in muscle are readily determined by 7Li imaging in vivo, and 2) the visibility of lithium in vivo is approximately 90% in brain regions and 100% in muscle.
the 7Li visibility of lithium in vivo in rat brain and rat muscle is about 80%, with a standard deviation of 10%.

the apparent concentration of lithium in vivo by 1H NMR imaging at high field is 10.1 +/- 1.0 mM for muscle and 4.1-5.3 +/- 0.4 mM for various brain areas in rats under dosing conditions used, and that the 7Li visibility of lithium in vivo is 96% +/- 2% for muscle and 74-93% +/- 3-6% for various brain regions in rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel approach to 7Li NQR imaging of lithium in vivo.
the use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to study the pharmacokinetics of the cationic drug lithium (Li) and the effects of Li on the brain in vivo.
the development of 7Li N-MR spectroscopy as a non-invasive method for the measurement of lithium concentrations in brain and muscle in living rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Li visibility is high but not perfect in vivo in the rat brain.
the apparent concentrations of Li determined by 7Li MRS and 7Li MRT in vivo are accurate to within 10% of the actual concentrations of the Li cations present in vivo.
the visibility of Li in vivo is essentially complete in muscle, and is probably complete in brain, but that there may be some uncertainty in this regard.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the apparent concentrations of Li in vivo by 1H-decoupled 7Li imaging at 4T are in reasonable agreement with concentrations of Li in tissue extracts by high-resolution 1H-decoupiled 7Li NQR spectroscopy, but that the 7Li visibility in vivo in the brain is reduced compared to that in muscle.
Li visibility in vivo is approximately 80% for brain tissue and approximately 100% for muscle tissue.
the visibility of the Li signal in vivo is 90-95%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the apparent Li concentration in vivo can provide useful estimates of the Li content of the brain and other tissues, provided that the visibility of the Li signal is accounted for.

the visibility of Li in brain and muscle tissue appears to be sufficiently high for the determination of the Li concentrations in these tissue regions in vivo by 1D 7Li MRI, and for the measurement of the time courses of Li concentrations during treatment with Li in these regions.
the 7Li visibility in brain tissue is not so different from that of Li in muscle, as has been suggested previously.
